newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS-Dow powers Tokyo/HK stocks, Manila hit again.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dow powers Tokyo/HK stocks, Manila hit again.

text.p: Tokyo and Hong Kong stock markets powered ahead on Wednesday, encouraged by Wall Street's rally overnight, but the gains were limited in other markets where sentiment remained generally negative.
Philippine stocks were hit again by fears of a shakeout in the property sector and expectations of poor corporate earnings.
A spate of U.S. economic data released on Tuesday turned out to be more favourable than anticipated and sent stocks and bonds soaring.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 179.01 points, or 2.64 percent, to 6,962.03 points -- marking the second-largest point rise in the history of the blue chip index.
The Dow's biggest gain in point terms remains a 186.84 point surge on October 21, 1987, two days after the so-called Black Monday market slump.
Bond prices surged as the news on the U.S. economy and inflation calmed fears the Federal Reserve might need to tighten interest rates at its next policy-making meeting in May.
The U.S. Treasury's benchmark 30-year bond gained 1-18/32, bringing the yield down to 6.98 percent.

When Tokyo trading resumed after Tuesday's national holiday, stocks surged, with the key 225-share Nikkei average surpassing the 19,000 level for the first time since February 28. At the close, the index was up 480.75 points or 2.57 percent at 19,151.12.

"The surge has erased one unclear factor that Tokyo has worried about," Seiki Orimi, manager of stock information services at Dai-Ichi Securities Co Ltd said in reference to the outlook for the U.S. market.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index closed the morning session up 284.83 points, or 2.26 percent, at 12,885.25.
Michael Ng, dealing director at Sassoon Securities, said sentiment had improved in both the United States and Hong Kong after the data were released.
The positive sentiment failed to carry over into the Philippines, which again fell victim to heavy selling.

Fear of weak corporate earnings and talk that the country's banking and property sectors may experience problems similar to those recently seen in Thailand pushed the Manila share index down another 60.27 points, or 2.23 percent, to end at 2,648.17 points.
That came on top of a 4.54 percent fall on Tuesday.
"Sentiment is very weak due to companies' profits that were below expectations," said Lawrence de Leon, analyst at Dharmala Securities Phils.
The Central Bank moved to calm investor fears, saying there was no capital flight after the stock market slump. It also raised the overnight borrowing interest rate to 11 percent from 10.25 percent.
"This is a preemptive move. This is just to calm the market," Central Bank Treasurer Sergio Edeza told Reuters.
Stocks in Taiwan also turned lower due to profit-taking, shedding 106.78 points or 1.24 percent to close at 8,485.66.
Elsewhere, the U.S. rally pushed other indices into the plus side, although the gains were capped by investor unease.
In Kuala Lumpur, the index rose 3.09 points or 0.29 percent to 1,062.6 in afternoon trading, while those in Singapore gained 9.16 points or 0.46 percent to 1,999.36.
"When the Dow is up it provides a slight cushion, and reduces the selling a bit," said Ami Moris, a vice president at Capitalcorp in Kuala Lumpur.
"We're still on a downward trend," she said. "I think it's premature to say we've seen the worst."
Australia's All Ordinaries Index closed at a preliminary 2,488, up 8.9 points or 0.36 percent.
Thai stocks rebounded from Tuesday's selloff, gaining 6.64 points or 1.01 percent to 665.23, while the Jakarta index was up 3.637 points or 0.56 percent to 650.867.
Korean shares were off 1.39 points at 702.66 in listless trading.
